blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular Position :- The angle made by the position vector w.r.t. origin, with the reference line is called angular position.

To decide the angular position of a point in space we need to specify origin and reference line.

Angular position depends on the choice of the origin as well as the reference line.

SI Unit: Radian

Relation between speed and Angular velocity :

$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A wheel starts from rest and undergoes uniform angular acceleration. After 10 seconds, its angular velocity is 20 rad/s. What is the angular position of the wheel at the end of 10 seconds?
blocks.answer:
Answer:
The angular position of the wheel after 10 seconds is 100 radians.

$\omega=\omega_0+\alpha t$

$\begin{gathered} 20=0+\alpha(10) \\ \alpha=\frac{20}{10}=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2 \end{gathered}$

$\theta=\omega_0 t+\frac{1}{2} \alpha t^2$

$\begin{gathered} \theta=0(10)+\frac{1}{2}(2)\left(10^2\right) \\ \theta=0+\frac{1}{2}(2)(100)=100 \text { radians } \end{gathered}$
blocks.prompt: A wheel starts from rest and undergoes uniform angular acceleration. After 10 seconds, its angular velocity is 20 rad/s. What is the angular position of the wheel at the end of 10 seconds?

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: The Earth rotates once every 24 hours. What is the angular position of a point on Earth's surface after 6 hours, assuming we start from 0° at noon?
blocks.answer:
Answer:
The angular position of the point on Earth's surface after 6 hours is 90° (eastward from the starting position).

• Time for one full revolution = 24 hours

  • Time elapsed = 6 hours
  • Full revolution = 360°
The Earth completes 360° in 24 hours. To find the angular position after 6 hours

$\text { Angular position }=\frac{6 \text { hours }}{24 \text { hours }} \times 360^{\circ}=0.25 \times 360^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular Displacement :- Angle through which the position vector of the moving particle rotates in a given time interval is called angular displacement.

Angular displacement depends on origin, but it does not depend on the reference line

  • Conventionally Clockwise Displacement is negative, anticlockwise is positive.
  • Angular displacement is an axial vector; its direction is along the axis of rotation, following the right-hand thumb rule.
  • Small angular displacement is a vector, but large angular displacement is not, as it doesn’t follow the commutative law of vector addition.
  • One complete revolution corresponds to  $2 \pi \text { radians. }$
  • For n revolutions, angular displacement $\theta=2 n \pi \text { radians. }$
$\text{Angular Displacement} = \frac{\text{arc}}{\text{radius}}$

$\Rightarrow \Delta \theta=\frac{\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{r}}$

• SI Unit : radian

$1 \text{ radian} = \frac{360^\circ}{2\pi}$=$\pi \text{ radians} = 180^\circ$

$\text { For } 1 \text { revolution, } \theta=2 \pi \mathrm{rad}$

• For $n$ revolutions, $\theta = 2n\pi \text{ radians}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A student runs 30 m around a circular track of diameter 100 m. What is his angular displacement?
blocks.answer:
After running 30 m, the student reaches point P at an angle θ as shown in the figure.

$\Delta \theta = \theta_2 - \theta_1$

$\theta_2 = \theta$

$\theta_2 = 0$

$\theta = \frac{\text{arc}}{\text{radius}}$

$\theta = \frac{30}{50} \, \text{rad}$

$\Delta \theta =0.6 $ Radian (Anticlockwise)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular Velocity$(\omega)$ :- It is defined as the rate of change of angular position of a moving particle with respect to time.

$(\omega)=$$\frac{d\theta}{dt}$

• Unit : Radian/sec

• Its dimension is [M0L0T–1]

Average angular velocity$(\omega_{\text{avg}})$$=\mathrm{\frac{Total~Angular~Displacement}{Total~Time~taken}}$=$\omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\theta_2 - \theta_1}{t_2 - t_1}$

Instantaneous Angular Velocity : $\frac{\mathbf{d} \vec{\theta}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

$(\omega_{\text{inst}})=\mathrm{\frac{component~of~velocity~perpendicular~to~line~joining}{length~of~line~joining}}=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{\perp}}{r}$

Relative Angular Velocity :-

The rate at which the position vector of 'A' w.r.t. B rotates at that instant.

$\omega=$$\frac{(V_{AB})_{\perp}}{r_{\text{AB}}}$=$\frac{\text{ relative velocity of A w.r.t B perpendicular to line AB}}{\text{separation  between  A      and B}}$

$(V_{AB})_{\perp}$=$=v_A \sin \theta_1 + v_B \sin \theta_2$

$\omega_{\text{AB}}$$=\frac{v_A \sin \theta_1 + v_B \sin \theta_2}{r}$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: Two moving particles P and Q are 5 m apart at any instant. Velocity of P is 10 m/s and that of Q is 15m/s. Calculate the angular velocity of P with respect to Q.
blocks.answer:
Angular velocity of P with respect to Q is

$\omega_{PQ}$=$\frac{(V_{PQ})_{\perp}}{r_{\text{PQ}}}$

$(V_{PQ})_{\perp}$=$6-(-12)=18m/s$

$r_{\text{PQ}}$=$5m$

$\omega_{PQ}$=$\frac{(V_{PQ})_{\perp}}{r_{\text{PQ}}}$=$\frac{18}{5}$ $radian/sec$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Angular Acceleration $(\alpha)$:- It is defined as rate of change of angular velocity with respect to time.

$\alpha=$$\frac{d\omega}{dt}$

Unit: $\text{rad/sec}^2$

Average angular acceleration$(\alpha_{\text{avg}})$ = $\dfrac{Change\ in\ angular ~velocity}{Total ~Time\ taken}$=$\dfrac{\vec \omega_f - \vec \omega_i}{t_2 - t_1}$=$\dfrac{\Delta \vec \omega}{\Delta t}$

Instantaneous angular acceleration$(\alpha_{\text{inst}})$ :-

It is the limit of average angular acceleration as $\Delta t$ approaches zero

$\overrightarrow{\alpha_{\text{inst}}} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \dfrac{\Delta \vec \omega}{\Delta t}$=$\dfrac{d \vec \omega}{dt}$

$\alpha=$$\frac{d\omega}{dt}$          {When  $\omega$ is a function of t }

$\alpha = \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}$                        {When $\theta$ is a function of t}

$\alpha = \omega \frac{d\omega}{d\theta}$                      {When $\omega $ is a function of $\theta$}

Acceleration in circular motion :-

• Tangential Acceleration :-
 Its magnitude is the rate of change of speed of the particle.

$a_T = \frac{\text{d} \left| \vec{v} \right|}{\text{d}t}$

• Centripetal Acceleration :-

The velocity of the particle changes while moving on the curved path, this change in velocity is brought by a force known as centripetal force and the acceleration so produced in the body is known as centripetal acceleration.

$\vec{a}_C=\vec{\omega} \times \vec{v}$

NOTE: Centripetal acceleration is always perpendicular to the velocity at each point , therefore it is responsible for change in direction of velocity.

$a_C = \omega^2 r$=$\frac{v^2}{r}$

• Net Acceleration :-

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{T}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{C}}$

$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_T^2 + a_C^2} = \sqrt{(\alpha r)^2 + \left(\frac{v^2}{r}\right)^2}$

$\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{T}}} \quad\left\{\theta \text { is the angle made by } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \text { with } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{T}}\right\}$

Important Points :-
(i) Differentiation of speed gives tangential acceleration.$$(ii) Differentiation of velocity $( \vec{v} )$ gives total acceleration.           $$

(iii) $ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| \& \frac{\mathrm{~d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}} $ are not same physical quantity. $\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| $ is the magnitude of rate of change of velocity, i.e. magnitude of total acceleration and  $\frac{\mathrm{d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}}$ is a rate of change of speed, i.e. tangential acceleration.
Here is the Hindi translation of the given explanation:

(iii)$ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| \& \frac{\mathrm{~d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}} $और एक जैसी भौतिक राशियाँ नहीं हैं।$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| $ वेग में परिवर्तन की दर का परिमाण है, अर्थात कुल त्वरण का परिमाण है। $\frac{\mathrm{d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}}$ गति (speed) में परिवर्तन की दर है, अर्थात अभिलंब (tangential) त्वरण है|

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A particle travels in a circle of radius 20 cm at a speed that uniformly increases. If the speed changes from 5.0 m/s to 6.0 m/s in 2.0 s, find the angular acceleration.
blocks.answer:
Since speed increases uniformly, average tangential acceleration is equal to instantaneous tangential

acceleration.

$a_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_2-\mathrm{v}_1}{t_2-t_1}=\frac{6.0-5.0}{2.0} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2=0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

$\alpha=\frac{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{T}}}{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2}{20 \mathrm{~cm}}=2.5 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2$

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question:
A particle is moving on a circular path of radius 5m and its time dependent angular position is, $\theta = \frac{t^3}{2} - \frac{t^2}{2}$radian. Find

(1) Angular displacement in first 3s

(2) Average angular velocity in first 3s

(3) Angular velocity at t = 2s

(4) Angular acceleration at t = 2s
blocks.answer:
(1) At  $t=0$ s,$\theta=0$ s

at

$t=3$ s

$\theta = \frac{3^3}{3} - \frac{3^2}{2}$=$9 - \frac{9}{2}$=4.5 radian

Angular displacement in first 3s =4.5 Radian

(2) $\omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{4.5 \, \text{rad}}{3 \, \text{s}} = \frac{3}{2} \, \text{rad/s}$

(3) $\omega_{\text{inst}} = \frac{d\theta}{dt} = \frac{3t^2}{3} - \frac{2t}{2}(t_2 - t)$

at t= 2, $\omega_{\text{inst}} = 2^2 - 2 = 2 \, \text{rad/sec}$

(4) $\alpha_{\text{inst}} = \frac{d\omega}{dt} = \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = 2t - 1$

at t=2 ,$\alpha = 2(2) - 1 = 3 \, \text{rad/sec}^2$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Centripetal Force: The force that is necessary to keep an object moving in a curved path and that is directed inward towards the centre of rotation.

$F_c=\frac{mv^2}{r}$=$m \omega^2 r$(Directed Inwards)

• Centrifugal Force : The apparent force that is felt by an object moving in a curved path that acts radially away from the center of rotation.

• Its magnitude is equal to centripetal force.

$F_{\text{cf}}=\frac{mv^2}{r}$(Radially Outwards)

Note: Centripetal force and centrifugal force are really the exact same force, just in opposite directions because they're experienced from different frames of reference.

• Tangential Force:  It is the force acting on a body in a circular motion in the tangential direction of a curved path.

• A tangential force is the follow up of a tangential acceleration which is always at right angle to the radius which originate from the axis of rotation.

$\vec{F}_T = m \vec{a}_T$

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question: A car of mass 1000 kg rounds a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. Determine the minimum frictional force required to prevent slipping.
blocks.answer:
Solution

  • Calculate centripetal force: $F_c=\frac{1000\times20^2}{50}=8000\,\text{N}$
  • Frictional force must be $\geq F_c$ to prevent slipping, so the minimum frictional force required is 8000 N.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Banking of roads - It is defined as the phenomenon in which the outer edges are raised for the curved roads above the inner edge to provide the necessary centripetal force to the vehicles so that they take a safe turn.

  • Friction between the tyres and the road provides the necessary centripetal force.
Case 1:

Circular turning on roads by friction only.

$v \leq \sqrt{ \mu r g}$

Case 2:

Circular turning on roads by banking of roads only.

$\tan \theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} = \frac{h}{b}$

Case 3:

a) Circular turning on roads by friction and banking of road both

$v < \sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$,then friction acts outwards

$v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{rg \tan(\theta - \phi)}$

b) If speed is high then friction acts inwards.

$v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{rg \tan(\theta + \phi)}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conical Pendulum:-

$v =\sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$

Angular speed = $\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \sqrt{\frac{g \tan \theta}{r}}$

So, the time period of pendulum is  $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{~g} \tan \theta}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{~L} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{~g}}}$

blocks.title: Death Well
blocks.text:
Death-Well or Rotor:- In death well, walls are at rest and person revolves while in case of rotor person is at rest w.r.t wall and the wall rotates.

Note: In both cases, friction balances the weight of person while reaction provides the centripetal force for circular motion.

$v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{\frac{gr}{\mu}}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A string breaks under a load of 50 kg. A mass of 1 kg is attached to one end of the string 10 m long and is rotated in horizontal circle. Calculate the greatest number of revolutions that the mass can make in one second without breaking the string.
blocks.answer:
$\omega=2 \pi \mathrm{f}, \mathrm{~T}_{\max }=500 \mathrm{~N}, \mathrm{r}=\mathrm{L} \sin \theta$

$\begin{gathered} T \sin \theta=m \omega^2 r \\ T=m \omega^2 L \end{gathered}$

$\mathrm{T}_{\max }=\mathrm{m} \omega_{\max }^2 \mathrm{~L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{~T}_{\max }=\mathrm{m}(2 \pi \mathrm{f})^2 \mathrm{~L}$

$\mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{~T}_{\max }}{\mathrm{mL}}}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{500}{1 \times 10}}=\frac{\sqrt{50}}{2 \pi} \text { revolution per second. }$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Vertical Circular Motion:- It Involves an object moving in a vertical circle. Gravity and tension are the main forces acting on the object.

Velocity at point P :-  $V = \sqrt{u^2 - 2gL(1 - \cos \theta)}$

Tension at Point P:-  $T = mg \cos \theta + \frac{mv^2}{L}$

1. At Point A (Bottom Point):-

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{A}}^2}{\mathrm{~L}}+\mathrm{mg} \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=0^{\circ}\right)$

2. At Point B :-

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{B}}{ }^2}{\mathrm{~L}}  \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=90^{\circ}\right)$

3. At Point C (Top Point) :-

$\mathrm{v_c}=\sqrt{\mathrm{u}^2-4 \mathrm{gL}}$

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{c}}^2}{\mathrm{~L}}-\mathrm{mg}  \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=180^{\circ}\right)$

4.   $T_{\text{bottom}} - T_{\text{top}} = 6mg$

Conditions For Looping The Loop :-

1. For looping the loop, velocity at lowest point must be $\geq \sqrt{5 \mathrm{gL}}$

2. Condition for looping for Massless Rod: $\text { For completing the loop } \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{L}} \geq \sqrt{4 \mathrm{gR}}$

3. Condition of Oscillation - $0 < u \leq \sqrt{2gL}$

4. Condition of Leaving the Circle-$\sqrt{2gL} < u < \sqrt{5gL}$

Note :- After leaving the circle, the particle will follow a parabolic path.

blocks.title: Question-1
blocks.question: The string of a pendulum is horizontal. The mass of the bob is m. Now the string is released. The tension at the string in the lowest position is
blocks.answer:
The situation is shown in fig. Let $v$ be the velocity of the bob at the lowest position. In this position the P.E. of bob is converted into K.E. hence

$mgL = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$

$v^2 = 2gL$.....(1)

If  $T$ be the tension in the string, then

$T - mg = \frac{m v^2}{l}$....(2)

from equation(1) and (2)

$T=3mg$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Using linear velocity formulas for angular velocity (or vice versa).
  • Mixing units like degrees/s with rad/s without proper conversion.
  • Assuming constant angular velocity when angular acceleration is present.
  • Ignoring the negative sign for clockwise rotation and only using magnitudes.
  • Not considering angular position when calculating angular velocity.

• Confusing Angular and Linear Quantities.
  • Not Accounting for Direction.
  • Forgetting to convert units for angular acceleration.

blocks.title: COMMON MISTAKES
blocks.text:
• Confusing centripetal and centrifugal forces: Remember, centripetal is real and acts towards the center; centrifugal is apparent and acts outward in a rotating frame.
    • Neglecting the frame of reference: Misinterpretation of forces due to not considering the correct frame can lead to errors.
    • Incorrect application of formulas: Ensure correct units and substitution in formulas, particularly distinguishing between linear and angular quantities.

Tip: Always draw a free-body diagram to visualize forces acting on the object.

blocks.title: COMMON MISTAKES
blocks.text:
• Misinterpretation of angles and neglecting friction.
  • Mixing units leading to incorrect calculations.
Key Tip: Always consider the direction and role of friction in providing or resisting centripetal force.

$\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{c}}}{\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{T}}} \quad\left\{\theta \text { is the angle made by } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \text { with } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{T}}\right\}$

Important Points :-
(i) Differentiation of speed gives tangential acceleration.$$(ii) Differentiation of velocity $( \vec{v} )$ gives total acceleration.           $$

(iii) $ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| \& \frac{\mathrm{~d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}} $ are not same physical quantity. $\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| $ is the magnitude of rate of change of velocity, i.e. magnitude of total acceleration and  $\frac{\mathrm{d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}}$ is a rate of change of speed, i.e. tangential acceleration.
Here is the Hindi translation of the given explanation:

(iii)$ \left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| \& \frac{\mathrm{~d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}} $और एक जैसी भौतिक राशियाँ नहीं हैं।$\left|\frac{\mathrm{d} \vec{v}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right| $ वेग में परिवर्तन की दर का परिमाण है, अर्थात कुल त्वरण का परिमाण है। $\frac{\mathrm{d}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}|}{\mathrm{dt}}$ गति (speed) में परिवर्तन की दर है, अर्थात अभिलंब (tangential) त्वरण है|

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Banking of roads - It is defined as the phenomenon in which the outer edges are raised for the curved roads above the inner edge to provide the necessary centripetal force to the vehicles so that they take a safe turn.

  • Friction between the tyres and the road provides the necessary centripetal force.
Case 1:

Circular turning on roads by friction only.

$v \leq \sqrt{ \mu r g}$

Case 2:

Circular turning on roads by banking of roads only.

$\tan \theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} = \frac{h}{b}$

Case 3:

a) Circular turning on roads by friction and banking of road both

$v < \sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$,then friction acts outwards

$v_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{rg \tan(\theta - \phi)}$

b) If speed is high then friction acts inwards.

$v_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{rg \tan(\theta + \phi)}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conical Pendulum:-

$v =\sqrt{rg \tan \theta}$

Angular speed = $\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \sqrt{\frac{g \tan \theta}{r}}$

So, the time period of pendulum is  $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{~g} \tan \theta}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{~L} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{~g}}}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Vertical Circular Motion:- It Involves an object moving in a vertical circle. Gravity and tension are the main forces acting on the object.

Velocity at point P :-  $V = \sqrt{u^2 - 2gL(1 - \cos \theta)}$

Tension at Point P:-  $T = mg \cos \theta + \frac{mv^2}{L}$

1. At Point A (Bottom Point):-

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{A}}^2}{\mathrm{~L}}+\mathrm{mg} \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=0^{\circ}\right)$

2. At Point B :-

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{B}}{ }^2}{\mathrm{~L}}  \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=90^{\circ}\right)$

3. At Point C (Top Point) :-

$\mathrm{v_c}=\sqrt{\mathrm{u}^2-4 \mathrm{gL}}$

$\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{c}}^2}{\mathrm{~L}}-\mathrm{mg}  \quad\left(\text { Here } \theta=180^{\circ}\right)$

4.   $T_{\text{bottom}} - T_{\text{top}} = 6mg$

Conditions For Looping The Loop :-

1. For looping the loop, velocity at lowest point must be $\geq \sqrt{5 \mathrm{gL}}$

2. Condition for looping for Massless Rod: $\text { For completing the loop } \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{L}} \geq \sqrt{4 \mathrm{gR}}$

3. Condition of Oscillation - $0 < u \leq \sqrt{2gL}$

4. Condition of Leaving the Circle-$\sqrt{2gL} < u < \sqrt{5gL}$

Note :- After leaving the circle, the particle will follow a parabolic path.
